source_text: Iam vero in ipsum Deum, pari fine, impari exordio, accusationum tela iaculantur. Manichaeus quippe dicit: Deus bonus malum non facit; sed addit quia pro naturalibus culpis aeterno incendio animas destinet; quod perspicuae immanitatis est: ac per hoc, fine opinionis suae, quem bonum dixerat, clara iniquitate contaminat. Porro Augustinus quasi ei ad quem scribit, fidens patrono, ausu grandiore despicit trepidationem magistri, nec dubitat inde incipere, quo Manichaeus pervenit; pronuntiatque quod malum, id est peccatum, faciat Deus et creet, quem constat non convenire ei Deo, quem Catholicorum fides colit. Hoc potissimum animo lectoris insidat, et nulli umquam fidelium maiorem causam quam nobis incubuisse conflictus, et omnem qui naturam ipsam necessitatem criminis arbitratur, in Dei Christianorum cultu non habere consortium; quod quoniam frequenter inculcatum est; iterationem quippe utilitas causae principalis exegit; veniamus iam ad discussionem primorum hominum, quorum taxatione aciei nostrae Numida quasi cetratus occurrit.
pass_a_gloss: Now indeed into God himself, with an equal end, an unequal beginning, they hurl the weapons of accusations. For Manichaeus says: A good God does not make evil; but he adds that for natural faults he destines souls to eternal fire; which is of a clear monstrosity: and through this, by the end of his opinion, he contaminates him whom he had said good with a clear iniquity. Further Augustine, as if trusting the patron to whom he writes, with a greater daring looks down on the teacher's trembling, nor does he doubt to begin from there where Manichaeus arrived; and he pronounces that God makes and creates evil, that is sin, whom it stands does not suit that God whom the faith of the Catholics worships. Let this especially sit in the reader's mind, both that a greater cause of conflict never hung over any of the faithful than over us, and that everyone who judges nature itself a necessity of a charge does not have fellowship in the cult of the Christians' God; which since it has been frequently impressed; for the utility of the principal cause demanded iteration; let us come now to the discussion of the first humans, by whose assessment the Numidian like a shield-bearer meets our battle-line.

pass_b_english: They now hurl their accusing weapons at God himself, reaching the same conclusion from different beginnings. Mani says: God is good and does no evil. But he adds that God consigns souls to eternal fire for natural faults—an act of obvious cruelty. Thus, at the end of his opinion, he stains with plain injustice the one he had called good.

Augustine, however, as though trusting the man he addresses as his patron, is bolder. He despises his teacher’s hesitation and does not hesitate to begin where Mani ended. He pronounces that God makes and creates evil—that is, sin. This plainly cannot fit the God worshiped by the catholic faith. Let this above all remain fixed in the reader’s mind: no believer has ever had a greater cause for struggle than ours, and anyone who considers nature itself a necessity for crime has no share in worshiping the Christians’ God. Since this has often been stressed—the usefulness of the central case required repetition—let us now examine the first humans, whose indictment the Numidian carries like a light shield when he meets our battle line.
